title: Derandomizing polynomial identity testing
formal: Is polynomial identity testing for explicitly represented arithmetic circuits over the integers in deterministic polynomial time? More precisely, do a deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) exist such that, on every valid circuit encoding of bit length \(N\), \(A\) decides whether the output is the zero formal polynomial and halts within \(C(N+2)^k\) steps?
why: Polynomial identity testing is a central concrete derandomization problem: a polynomial may be identically zero because of cancellations invisible in the circuit syntax. A deterministic polynomial-time test would affect symbolic computation and numerous algebraic algorithms, and is known to imply major circuit lower bounds. This places the question at the intersection of efficient verification of algebraic identities and fundamental complexity limitations.
status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. The original source explicitly identifies the circuit version as unresolved. The 2026 primary papers retain the general PIT question and supply reductions or restricted-model progress, rather than a general deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. No matching proof or refutation was found in the bounded search; cited proofs were not independently verified.

importance.reason: A defining derandomization problem for unrestricted arithmetic circuits, with broad algebraic-algorithm applications and proved consequences for Boolean or arithmetic circuit lower bounds. The general explicit-circuit target is substantially broader than the many restricted circuit classes for which deterministic tests are known.

sentences: An arithmetic circuit may compute the zero polynomial even when cancellation is difficult to see from its graph.
The question asks for an exact deterministic polynomial-time test given the entire circuit over binary-encoded integer constants.
Circuits may reuse intermediate results, have arbitrary depth and compute polynomials of exponential degree.
Randomized polynomial-time tests are known, while removing their randomness would have major circuit lower-bound consequences.
Recent deterministic results for restricted circuit shapes do not provide the requested algorithm for all explicit circuits.

definitions: An arithmetic circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output. Each input node is either one of the explicitly listed variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) or a signed integer constant given in binary. Each internal gate has two ordered predecessors and computes addition, subtraction or multiplication over \(\mathbb Z\). Intermediate results may be used by several later gates; the graph need not be a formula. A topological list of all nodes, their labels, predecessor indices and the output index is supplied, with the full variable list and all bits of every constant included in the input length \(N\). Repeated use of a variable or predecessor is allowed. Gates compute in the commutative polynomial ring \(\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), and the zero polynomial means that every coefficient is exactly zero. No division, exponentiation, comparison, oracle or approximate-arithmetic gate is present. There is no depth restriction, multilinearity promise or bound on the number of nonzero monomials. No separate polynomial bound on total degree is promised: repeated multiplication can give a degree exponential in the circuit description length. The algorithm has access to the complete graph and labels, not only an oracle for evaluations. Its running time counts bit-level Turing-machine operations, including all work on constants and any integers it computes; unbounded-size integer operations are not free. Correctness is exact on every valid encoding, with no randomness or advice. Malformed encodings are rejected within the same polynomial bound. One fixed machine and one fixed polynomial bound must work for all numbers of variables, circuits, degrees and integer constants.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm exists, or prove that no such algorithm exists in the stated bit model. A positive answer requires a uniform algorithm correct for every allowed circuit, including those of exponential degree. A negative answer must exclude every deterministic machine with any fixed polynomial time bound; a lower bound for one procedure does not suffice. Results only for formulas, restricted depth, bounded-read circuits, sparse polynomials or a restricted degree regime do not resolve the full target. An evaluation-only lower bound without the explicit circuit-description promise also does not refute it. Numerical agreement at sampled inputs does not establish a formal identity.

context_blocks.text: Two very different circuit expressions can represent the same polynomial. For instance, \((x+y)^2-x^2-2xy-y^2\) is zero as a formal polynomial. Identity testing asks for this conclusion without first expanding an expression that may contain exponentially many monomials.

The circuit description is part of the input. Its reuse of intermediate values can compress a large polynomial into a small graph, but the algorithm may inspect that graph. This differs from access only to a polynomial’s values, without any representation-size promise.

Strozecki’s enumeration survey explicitly identifies deterministic polynomial-time identity testing for arithmetic-circuit representations as a major unresolved step. The discussion explains why identity tests arise in procedures that generate the monomials of an implicitly represented polynomial.

The card adopts the standard integer-circuit, bit-complexity version of that direction, as explicitly defined in the 2026 STACS paper. Binary integer constants are included with their encoding cost. The target neither gives free arbitrary field constants nor silently bounds the circuit’s degree.

Randomized polynomial-time identity testing is known with one-sided error: the zero polynomial is always recognized as zero, while a nonzero polynomial is rejected with a fixed probability bounded away from zero. The requested change is a fully deterministic, all-input guarantee in polynomial time.

Kabanets and Impagliazzo prove that a polynomial-time deterministic identity test would force a major lower bound for Boolean circuits or for arithmetic circuits computing the permanent. This implication explains why removing randomness here is consequential. It does not make the task identical to proving any one chosen arithmetic lower bound.

Černý and Seppelt’s 2026 work shows that the same general identity-testing problem governs certain equivalence questions for graphs and weighted tree automata. Their reductions retain identity testing as a derandomization condition; they do not supply the requested deterministic test.

Shpilka and Tal’s February 2026 preprint gives deterministic identity tests for special expressions \(\sum_{i=1}^{r} f_i^d\), where the \(f_i\) are sparse low-degree polynomials and the common power \(d\) is sufficiently large relative to \(r\). The input structure and parameter conditions are essential, and its polynomial bounds in those degree parameters do not cover all circuits in time polynomial in their bit length.
